# Introduction {#sec-introduction}

A large experimental and survey literature finds that forecasts respond too much to recent news. @afrouzi2023overreaction show subjects series generated by a first-order autoregression, $x_t = \rho x_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t$, with the persistence ρ fixed per subject, and ask for forecasts. Regressing a subject's forecast on the current value gives an *implied persistence*: above ρ, the forecast moves too much with the latest value (overreaction); below ρ, too little (underreaction). People's implied persistence lies above ρ for every ρ below one, by more when ρ is low. In survey data the same question is asked with the regression of forecast errors on forecast revisions [@coibion2015information; @bordalo2020overreaction]. In both traditions the reference point is the forecast of someone who knows the data-generating process.

That reference point is demanding. A forecaster who does not know ρ and learns it from the data is unbiased only on average over its prior. At any fixed ρ its posterior is pulled towards the prior, so its implied persistence sits above ρ when ρ is low and below ρ when ρ is high. Part of the human pattern, more overreaction when persistence is low, is therefore what a rational learner does anyway. A forecaster who sees only the last W observations is pulled further, because it has less data. A deviation from the full-information forecast, or even from the full-sample Bayes forecast, is thus not evidence of a bias: it may be the information the forecaster lacks. The informative comparison is with the Bayes forecaster that holds the same prior *and the same information*. The pre-registration of this study states the rule in one sentence: "{{< var prereg.bias_rule >}}"

This paper applies that rule to artificial forecasters for which the comparison can be made exact. We train causal transformers from scratch, with no objective but squared forecast error, on simulated AR(1) sequences whose persistence is drawn afresh from U[0, 1] for every sequence. The networks come in {{< var design.n_sizes >}} sizes and with {{< var design.n_windows >}} memory lengths, W = {{< var design.windows_finite >}} observations or the full sequence, where a memory length is a hard limit on the input and not a property of the attention pattern. For each network we compute the exact Bayes forecast under the training prior from exactly the observations the network sees, which we call *window-Bayes* (@sec-environment). With the mean and the noise scale known, implied persistence at ρ = 0 is {{< var bench.bayes.r00 >}} for Bayes and {{< var bench.w4.r00 >}} for a Bayesian with four observations; at ρ = 0.8 it is {{< var bench.bayes.r08 >}} and {{< var bench.w4.r08 >}} (@fig-benchmarks). The windowed Bayesian overreacts against the truth at low persistence and underreacts at high persistence, without any bias at all.

That gives a sharp question. People in the experiment overreact against the truth at high persistence too (implied persistence {{< var human.r08.ip >}} at ρ = 0.8). Does a network trained only on squared error ever overreact where the information-matched Bayesian underreacts, at ρ = {{< var design.h3.rho_lo >}} and {{< var design.h3.rho_hi >}}? With the mean and the scale known, rational learning under the same prior cannot produce that; if a network did, the cause would lie in the architecture or the optimisation, and it would be a candidate mechanism for the human pattern.

One point of theory fixes what such an experiment can show. The forecast that minimises expected squared error, given the last W observations and the time index, is the posterior mean under the training prior, which is window-Bayes (@prp-optimal). A network that can represent it and optimised perfectly would match it by construction. The hypotheses therefore do not ask whether a rational forecast is optimal; they ask whether a finite network trained by stochastic gradient descent reaches that optimum, and whether what remains when it does not points in the human direction. The question is empirical because nothing guarantees that training gets there, and the smallest model and the earlier checkpoints reported below show that it need not.

The paper makes three contributions, stated here with their limits.

First, it builds an *information-matched benchmark* and measures the diagnostics of the expectations literature against it. Window-Bayes conditions on exactly the network's inputs, including the marginal likelihood of the first observation in the window given its time index; the implied-persistence gap, excess squared error and error-on-revision coefficient are then measured in excess of that benchmark, not in excess of the truth (@sec-environment). Matching the optimal filter in squared error is established for transformers [@balim2023can; @akram2024transformers], and our H1 is close to a replication of it. That a Bayesian learner fails full-information tests at a fixed parameter is not new either [@lewellen2002learning; @farmer2024learning]. What the benchmark adds is the separation of an information limit from a learning failure, in the units in which human overreaction is reported; the part of the argument that rests on the benchmarks alone (@fig-benchmarks) does not depend on any network.

Second, it maps that comparison across *memory length and model size*: {{< var design.n_windows >}} windows and {{< var design.n_sizes >}} sizes, {{< var runs.planned >}} training runs in all, each scored on the same fixed evaluation sets at {{< var design.n_rho >}} values of ρ and {{< var design.horizons >}} horizons (@sec-networks). Only the largest size enters a decision; the others, the training-time traces and the longer horizons are reported as exploratory (@sec-exploratory).

Third, the *decision rules were fixed in advance*, which is what lets an equivalence and a null be reported as results and not as failures to find something. The rows each hypothesis reads, two-sided equivalence margins, a Bonferroni rule for H3 and a rule separating under-training from bias by re-training at twice the length were frozen in a tagged pre-registration before any confirmatory run (@sec-prereg, [Appendix @sec-app-prereg]). The pre-registration is the author's own tagged document; it was not lodged with a registry, and @sec-prereg and [Appendix @sec-app-deviations] state exactly what was fixed when.

The results are these. H1 is {{< var h1.decision >}} (@sec-h1): the largest model with the full window is equivalent to Bayes on {{< var h1.n_equivalent >}} of {{< var h1.n_total >}} verdicts. For H2 (@sec-h2), the decision at each of W = {{< var design.windows_finite >}} is "{{< var h2.w2.decision >}}", the registered label for equivalence to window-Bayes on every verdict. H3 is {{< var h3.decision >}} (@sec-h3): {{< var h3.statement >}}, and the largest upper end of a {{< var design.level_pct >}}% interval is {{< var h3.max_hi >}} against the threshold of {{< var design.h3.threshold >}}. No finding was flagged, so the pre-registered re-training at {{< var design.steps_long >}} steps was not run. The intervals, and how far inside the margins they lie, are in the sections named.

Four qualifications belong beside those results, and each is developed in @sec-limitations. The verdicts hold at step {{< var design.steps >}}, the last checkpoint, when the cosine learning rate has decayed to zero; at {{< var design.step_mid >}} steps the windowed models are equivalent on at most {{< var trace.windowed.max_equivalent_early >}} of {{< var h2.n_total >}} verdicts per window (exploratory; @sec-exploratory). The smallest model departs from its benchmarks, towards a middling persistence. The evidence is one architecture on simulated AR(1) data. And because window-Bayes is the squared-error optimum, the finding is that training reached it, with no residual in the human direction; it is not a finding about people. The descriptive overlay of @sec-overlay makes the last point concrete: with the mean and scale unknown, the matched Bayesian itself overreacts at high persistence, and the human intervals include the four-observation Bayes curve from ρ = {{< var overlay.first_rho_incl_w4 >}} upward, so the overlay does not show people overreacting beyond an information-limited Bayesian.

The paper proceeds as follows. @sec-literature places the study between the literature on transformers as optimal filters and the literature on expectations tests applied to machine forecasters. @sec-environment sets out the two data-generating families, the benchmarks and the diagnostics, and proves that window-Bayes is the squared-error optimum. @sec-networks describes the networks, training and evaluation. @sec-prereg gives the pre-registration, the hypotheses in their registered wording and the decision rules. Sections [-@sec-h1], [-@sec-h2] and [-@sec-h3] report the three hypotheses, each with its confirmatory table. @sec-exploratory reports the exploratory results, @sec-overlay the descriptive human overlay and @sec-spf an illustrative comparison with professional forecasters. @sec-limitations discusses what the design cannot establish and @sec-conclusion concludes. The appendices reproduce the pre-registration ([Appendix @sec-app-prereg]), every deviation and decision ([Appendix @sec-app-deviations]), the disclosures ([Appendix @sec-app-disclosures]), every verdict with its seed values ([Appendix @sec-app-verdicts]), the data and replication record ([Appendix @sec-app-replication]) and supplementary tables and figures ([Appendix @sec-app-supplementary]).
